args: Web accessibility patterns as DESIGN-TIME decisions, not code fixes. Narrow scope — four tightly related topics only. (1) The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG): which of its patterns encode decisions a designer makes rather than a developer — specifically disclosure vs accordion vs tabs, dialog vs alertdialog, combobox vs listbox vs select, menu vs menubar vs toolbar, and treegrid vs grid vs table — and what visual and interaction commitments each pattern obliges once chosen (expected keyboard model, focus behavior, visible state). (2) The "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA" rule from the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices and the five rules of ARIA use — concrete named cases where ARIA is the WRONG answer and a native element or a layout change is correct instead, and the specific measured harm bad ARIA causes to screen reader users; cite WebAIM Million data on ARIA correlating with higher detected error rates if it exists. (3) Focus management on route change and view transitions in single-page applications — what the accepted correct behavior is when a route changes, where focus should go, the role of a skip link and a page-title announcement, how the View Transitions API interacts with focus and with prefers-reduced-motion, and the known failure of focus being lost to document body. (4) Live regions and aria-live for asynchronous results — aria-live polite vs assertive, role=status vs role=alert, aria-atomic and aria-relevant, the requirement that the live region exist in the DOM before content is injected, and documented cross-screen-reader failure modes across NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver. Prioritize primary and authoritative sources only: w3.org WAI ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, W3C ARIA specification, WebAIM articles and the WebAIM Million report, and TPGi or Deque technical writeups where W3C is silent. Reject generic blog restatements.
